newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Mercenary group winds down Sierra Leone mission.
newsitem.headline: Mercenary group winds down Sierra Leone mission.

text.p: South African mercenary group Executive Outcomes leaves Sierra Leone on Monday after more than 20 months of backing the army against rebels, the group's commander said.
"The lot of them have gone already and the remainder will be leaving on Monday. Only three or four people will be left behind to wind down the accounts," Brigadier Burt Sachse told Reuters on Sunday.
Sachse did not say how many of the South Africans would be on the flight home on the company's own aircraft, but military sources put the number at about 30.

The then military government in Freetown turned to the Pretoria-based firm in May 1995 after rebels who launched a campaign in 1991 overran key bauxite and diamond mining centres and started attacking close to the capital.
At the height of their operation the mercenaries numbered about 300 and included some fighters from Angola, where the group first backed UNITA rebels and then the government army.

They helped train Sierra Leone's ineffective army, which retook the initiative in the war and forced the Revolutionary United Front rebels to negotiate. Executive Outcomes also assured security at important mining sites.
Although a U.N. force of about 700 is due to monitor the accord in the West African country, security worries loom again after the govrenment's announcement of three coup plots in four months.
Amid allegations of truce violations by the government and rebels, mining companies who braved the civil war and stayed are considering alternative security arrangements.
Sachse, however, sounded optimistic when asked last month about the departure of Executive Outcomes, a key demand of the rebels that blocked negotiations for months.

"There is no longer a requirement for an offensive force in the land," he told Reuters. "I believe the government is quite capable of handling its own internal security problem. We must now leave the country".
Security fears continue to hamper the full-scale return of foreign investors to Sierra Leone, essential for the recovery of the mining-based economy.
President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah who negotiated the peace accord with rebel leader Foday Sankoh repeated his government's assurances in a speech on January 2.
"To the international community and any potential investors to Sierra Leone I say there is nothing to be concerned about. All is well," he said after the latest coup plot news.

Despite helping to quicken the end of the war that killed about 20,000 people and made hundreds of thousands homeless, controversy has dogged the activities of Executive Outcomes in Sierra Leone and elsewhere in Africa. The Sierra Leone contract ended officially last Friday and was not renewed.

Although Executive Outcomes seeks to promote the security side of its operations, the mercenary stigma has stuck on the group, more so for its switching of allegiances between rebels and the government in the Angola war.

Donors expected to fund Sierra Leone's reconstruction and rehabilitation queried the millions of dollars paid by the state to the group. Sierra Leone is widely believed to have settled part of the bill through mining concessions.
